what_it_does: Running a large language model (an AI that generates text) on a small edge device — a phone or embedded system — is hard because the model keeps a large 'running notes' table (called a key-value cache) that stores context from every word seen so far, quickly filling the device's limited memory. VEDA attacks this with three coordinated ideas: first, a voting scheme where different parts of the model collectively decide which cached entries are least important and can be safely discarded; second, a hardware processing unit whose internal data-routing paths can be reconfigured at runtime to handle the varying sizes of matrix operations that arise as sequence length changes; and third, a step-by-step schedule for nonlinear operations (calculations that are not pure multiply-add, such as computing a normalized probability distribution over a large set of options) that avoids storing large intermediate results. Together these bring memory needs from growing proportionally with sequence length down to a fixed, constant footprint, which the paper claims without full quantitative breakdown in the abstract.
